title: SPG: Sandwiched Policy Gradient for Masked Diffusion Language Models
one_liner: Use two honest estimates of how good an answer is (one too high, one too low) to teach a language model via reward signals.
lead: Diffusion language models generate words by gradually unmasking letters in parallel, making them faster than traditional word-by-word models. But teaching them to follow human feedback or task rewards is stuck: standard reward-based learning does not work because the model's true success score (log-likelihood) is hidden and intractable. SPG solves this by building two bounds around that true score—one that overestimates and one that underestimates—and uses both to train.

problem.h2: Why reward learning for diffusion models is broken
paras: Diffusion language models work like a artist filling in a portrait gradually: start with every pixel masked (hidden), then step by step unmask real words until a complete sentence appears. They are fast because many words unmask in parallel, not one at a time like traditional models.

To make them follow human preferences or solve tasks, we want to use reinforcement learning (RL)—reward good answers, penalize bad ones. But here is the trap: RL methods need to know exactly how likely each answer is, measured on a clear scale. For diffusion models, that true likelihood is buried deep in the math and too expensive to compute directly. Prior work punts: they use a one-sided guess (the ELBO, an estimate from pre-training) pretending it is the true score. But a one-sided guess biases the learning, especially when punishing bad outputs.

callout.html: SPG builds both an overestimate and an underestimate of how good an answer is, then uses both to train, eliminating the bias of a one-sided guess.

steps.b: Start with a pre-trained diffusion model
steps.text: The model is trained to unmask sequences but not yet tuned to follow rewards.

steps.b: Sample multiple completions and grade them
steps.text: For each prompt, sample several candidate answers and score each with a reward function (e.g., task accuracy).

steps.b: Compute advantage (did this answer beat the average)
steps.text: For each completion, compute how much better or worse it is than the average of the samples, because this tells the model which answers to emphasize and which to discourage relative to typical performance.

steps.b: Build upper and lower bounds of likelihood
steps.text: Instead of one guess, compute two: a score that overestimates and a score that underestimates the true success.
Mix the two bounds to form an unbiased estimate, then update the model's weights to increase scores for good answers.

object.h2: The one thing the paper changes
paras: The paper changes how the model learns from rewards. Instead of using a single biased estimate of answer quality (the ELBO), it swaps in a mixture of an upper and lower bound. This mixture is unbiased (not systematically too high or too low) because one bound is provably too high and the other too low, so their average cancels the bias, allowing the model to learn the right lesson from each reward.

hidden.name: Upper and lower bounds of log-likelihood
paras: The core challenge is computing the true log-likelihood (how likely the model assigns to each answer). This is intractable—too expensive to calculate directly. SPG works around this by computing two approximations: an upper bound (an estimate that is provably too high) and a lower bound (an estimate that is provably too low). The truth lies between them.

Prior work used only the lower bound (ELBO), biasing the learning. SPG computes both, then mixes them. The paper estimates the bounds using block-wise masking: corrupt chunks of the sequence at random, predict the missing parts, and use this prediction to derive an evidence upper bound (EUBO).

heat.caption: Darker means higher bounds or stronger signal. Highlighted cells are core to SPG.

reads.html: The paper measures whether answers are truly good using two honest estimates (one too optimistic, one too pessimistic), then averages them to get an unbiased signal. This prevents the model from learning a distorted view of which answers to prefer.

SPG computes the Evidence Upper Bound (EUBO) using one-step predictions on block-wise masked sequences, then mixes it with the pre-training ELBO in an advantage-weighted objective. The mixture weight ω is adapted per weight to minimize variance, ensuring stable and accurate weight updates.

paras: When you train a model with rewards, you nudge the weights in a direction that increases the score for good answers and decreases it for bad ones. But that nudge must be *correct*—it should point toward answers the reward function truly likes. If your score estimate is biased (always too high or always too low), the nudge goes in the wrong direction.

SPG's trick: use two estimates that bracket the truth. The upper bound (EUBO) overestimates; the lower bound (ELBO) underestimates. When you mix them, their biases cancel out, giving an unbiased estimate. This means the training nudge points in the right direction. Moreover, SPG adapts the mixture weight for each weight in the model—some weights benefit from trusting the upper bound more, others trust the lower bound more. This per-weight adaptation further reduces noise in the weight-update direction, making training stable and efficient.

stages.s: Mask random blocks of the sequence
Compute upper bound (EUBO from one-step prediction)
Mix bounds with adaptive weight per weight
Compute weight-update direction using mixture and reward advantage
Updated weights that favor high-reward answers

math.words: Gradient from mixture equals (one-minus-mixture-weight times lower-bound weight) plus (mixture-weight times upper-bound measure), all multiplied by the change in log-likelihood of the answer

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a weight w1 has ELBO weight w(t)=0.8 and upper-bound measure ρ_β=1.2.
Optimal mixture for this weight is ω=0.5 (balancing both equally).
With ω=0: gradient would be 0.8*(change), biased low. With ω=1: 1.2*(change), biased high. ω=0.5 gives unbiased 1.0.

math.note: The mixture weight ω is adapted per weight to minimize variance in the gradient, ensuring the nudge is stable.

bars.h2: How SPG compares to ELBO-based methods

charts.title: ELBO-only baseline (biased one-sided guess)
charts.note: Using only the lower bound ELBO creates systematic bias. The model learns a skewed preference.

charts.title: SPG (sandwiched unbiased bounds)
charts.note: Mixing upper and lower bounds removes bias. The model learns true preferences, improving reasoning and logic tasks.

items.html: If the masked blocks are too large, the model cannot predict the missing words accurately, breaking the upper-bound estimate. The blocks must be sized to the model's capacity.

If the upper and lower bounds diverge wildly (e.g., one is 10x the other), the adaptive mixture weight ω can become extreme and unstable, amplifying noise. This happens when the model sees data very different from what it was trained on.

The paper shows that negative-advantage penalties are critical. Without them, the model does not learn to avoid bad outputs, only to chase good ones. Removing negative-reward pressure causes a large performance drop.

items.b: Done right: block size tuned to model capacity, mixture weight constrained, and negative rewards included.
items.html: SPG works when all three pieces are in place: block-wise masking that the model can reason about, variance-minimizing mixture weight per layer, and explicit penalties for bad outputs.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: To show SPG works, build a small diffusion model (or use a pre-trained one at reduced size) and fine-tune it on a simple reward task like GSM8K math problems. Compare three training runs: (1) ELBO-only baseline, (2) upper-bound-only baseline, (3) SPG with both bounds. Track the reward score over training steps and measure final accuracy on held-out math problems. SPG converges faster because the unbiased mixture estimate has lower variance than either one-sided bound alone, so each training step nudges the model more confidently. SPG reaches higher accuracy because the unbiased estimate prevents the model from learning false preferences: a one-sided guess biases the learning direction, causing the model to chase phantom reward signals.
demo.metric_eq: Accuracy on math problems = number correct / total problems; Convergence speed = steps to 90% of final accuracy
demo.closing: The demo must make it impossible to miss that both bounds together (SPG) learn better and faster than either bound alone, because canceling the bias and reducing variance both matter for training efficiency and final performance.
